processing: A boiled drink: tea is cooked directly in milk, without water, usually with sugar and often whole spices, then strained.
harvest_season: Not tied to a harvest; made all year from everyday black tea.
appearance_dry: The base is plain everyday black tea, as is usual for South Asian milk teas.
appearance_wet: Leaf and spices are strained out before serving.
taste_profile: Thick and rich from whole milk, sweetened to taste and warm with cardamom and ginger when spiced.

brewing.notes: The volume here is full-cream milk, not water. Bring milk and any spices to the boil, add tea, simmer gently, then sweeten and strain.

vintage_note: Made fresh at home, at dhabas and by chaiwalas, so it has no year or season. Any everyday black tea will do. It costs slightly more than water-based chai because it uses only milk.
description:
Doodh pati chai means milk leaf tea, and the name tells you the point: the tea cooks in milk, with no water to dilute it. That separates it from saada chai, the water-based everyday tea, and makes it slightly dearer.

A common method brings full-cream milk to the boil with spices such as green or black cardamom, ginger, cinnamon, pepper, cloves or fennel, and sometimes saffron. Tea goes in next, sugar to taste, and the pot simmers on low until it thickens a bit before straining.

The result is rich and sweet, with the tea still clearly there under the milk. Milk mutes tea, so people who find theirs bland usually need more leaf or a longer simmer rather than more spice.

You will find it at dhabas and chaiwalas as well as at home, mainly across Pakistan and northern India, and occasionally in Nepal and Bangladesh. It has also spread to the Middle East. Some people still sip it from the saucer's edge in the old way.
history:
The drink comes from the Indian subcontinent, but little is documented about when it took shape, and no inventor is recorded. The name joins the Hindi and Urdu words for milk and leaf with chai, a word that reached these languages through Persian from Chinese.

It is sold at roadside dhabas and by chaiwalas, though it is most often made at home. It has also spread to the Middle East.
